info.name: Tribeca Jets Command Center API
info.description:
Auth and CRM endpoints for the Tribeca Jets Command Center.

## Authentication

Sessions live entirely in **httpOnly cookies**. No token is ever returned in a
response body, so there is nothing to paste into an Authorization header — and
no Bearer auth is configured on this collection on purpose.

Postman keeps cookies in its own jar, so once you run **01 · Auth → 01 · Login**
the rest of the collection is authenticated.

> Using Postman on the **web**? Install the Postman Desktop Agent first, or the
> cookie jar stays empty and every authenticated request returns 401.

| Cookie | httpOnly | Path | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tj_access` | yes | `/` | 15-minute access token |
| `tj_refresh` | yes | `/api/auth` | 7-day (30 with Remember me) refresh token |
| `tj_csrf` | **no** | `/` | Read by JS, echoed in `X-CSRF-Token` |
| `tj_2fa` | yes | `/api/auth` | In-flight two-factor challenge |
| `tj_pwreset` | yes | `/api/auth` | In-flight password-reset challenge |

## CSRF

Cookies are attached automatically by the client, so every **POST / PATCH /
DELETE** must also send `X-CSRF-Token`. The collection captures the readable
`tj_csrf` cookie into `{{csrfToken}}` after any response that sets one, and the
write requests reference it. Run a login first and this is invisible.

## The 6-digit codes

Two-factor and password-reset codes are emailed. **While SMTP is unconfigured**
(and outside production) the API also returns the code in a `devCode` object, so
the OTP flows work with no mailbox:

```json
"devCode": {
  "code": "481920",
  "notice": "SMTP is not configured, so no email was sent..."
}
```

The relevant requests copy that into `{{otpCode}}` automatically. Set
`SMTP_HOST`, `SMTP_USER` and `SMTP_PASSWORD` and `devCode` disappears — real
email is sent instead, and you paste the code into `{{otpCode}}` yourself.
Production refuses to boot without SMTP, so this can never leak from a real
deployment.

## Two-factor is per account

`user.twoFactorEnabled` is a per-account setting the Settings screen toggles,
not a global switch. `POST /auth/login` returns `requiresTwoFactor` and the
frontend branches on it — accounts with 2FA off go straight to the dashboard.

## Response shape

Success is always `{ success: true, data, meta? }`; `meta` appears on list
endpoints. Errors are always:

```json
{ "success": false, "statusCode": 400, "message": "Validation failed",
  "errors": { "email": "Invalid email address" },
  "path": "/api/auth/login", "timestamp": "..." }
```

Every request below carries saved examples for its success case **and each of
its error cases** — all captured from the live API, not hand-written.

## Variable scoping

Environments carry only `baseUrl`. Runtime values (`csrfToken`, `otpCode`,
`clientId`) are **collection** variables. Adding a same-named key to an
environment would shadow whatever the scripts write, and `{{csrfToken}}` would
silently resolve to empty — making every write 403.

## Running the whole collection

Folders execute top to bottom and are ordered so a full pass works: sign-in
establishes the session, Clients exercises CRUD, password reset comes after
(completing it revokes every session), sign-out is near the end, and the
regression folder asserts an unauthenticated caller is rejected.

```bash
npm run test:api
```

## Seeded accounts (development)

| Email | Password | Role | 2FA |
|---|---|---|---|
| admin@tribecajets.com | ChangeMe123! | SUPER_ADMIN | off |
| broker@tribecajets.com | ChangeMe123! | BROKER | off |
| security@tribecajets.com | ChangeMe123! | ADMIN | **on** |
| reset-demo@tribecajets.com | ChangeMe123! | BROKER | off |

`reset-demo` exists purely as the password-reset target. Re-run `npm run db:seed`
to restore its password after exercising folder 04.

item.name: 01 · Auth
item.description:
Every `/auth/*` route, grouped by the frontend screen that calls it.

| Frontend route | Sub-folder | Endpoint |
|---|---|---|
| `/sign-in` | 01 · Sign in | `POST /auth/login` |
| `/sign-in/two-factor` | 02 · Two-factor | `POST /auth/two-factor/verify` · `/resend` |
| `/sign-in/complete` | — | no API call; the session already exists |
| `/forgot-password` | 04 · Password reset | `POST /auth/forgot-password` |
| `/forgot-password/verify` | 04 · Password reset | `POST /auth/forgot-password/verify` · `/resend` |
| `/reset-password` | 04 · Password reset | `POST /auth/reset-password` |
| `/reset-password/success` | — | no API call |
| every authenticated page | 03 · Session | `GET /auth/me`, `POST /auth/refresh` |
| sign-out control | 05 · Sign out | `POST /auth/logout` |

**Not yet built:** the two-factor screen offers *"Trouble signing in? Use a backup code instead"*, but no backup-code endpoint exists. Either drop that line from the UI or scope the feature (generate at enrolment, store hashed, single-use, regenerate from Settings).

Also settings-module work, deliberately outside auth: the toggle that flips `twoFactorEnabled`, and change-password for a signed-in user.

item.name: 01 · Sign in
item.description:
One sign-in per role, so every account the collection uses is documented in one place and the rest of the collection never repeats an auth endpoint.

All five share the password `ChangeMe123!`. Each stores `csrfToken` for manual use; the module folders get their own session from a pre-request script and do not depend on running these first.

`02 · Admin · two-factor` is the odd one out — it returns a challenge rather than a session, and needs `02 · Two-factor / 02 · Verify code` to complete.

exec: // Every folder below gets its session from a pre-request script, but a
// login run by hand should still leave the collection usable.

request.description:
The seeded owner. Holds every permission, and is the one account that cannot be demoted, suspended or removed — so the system can never be locked out of its own administration.

Use this for the Users and Clients folders.

**Sets three cookies**, all httpOnly except the last:

| Cookie | Lifetime | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `tj_access` | 15 minutes | the session |
| `tj_refresh` | 7 days, or 30 with `rememberMe` | rotates the session |
| `tj_csrf` | matches refresh | echoed back as `X-CSRF-Token` on writes |

No token is ever returned in the body. The browser attaches them automatically and frontend JavaScript cannot read the first two.

item.name: 03 · Session
item.description: Called from every authenticated page. `GET /auth/me` is how the frontend learns who is signed in, since the token is httpOnly and unreadable by JavaScript.

request.description:
Who is signed in. With httpOnly cookies the frontend cannot decode a token, so this endpoint is the session's source of truth.

**`permissions` is the caller's row of the permission matrix**, as `{ PERMISSION: Scope }`. The UI reads it to avoid offering actions the guard would refuse — a role seeing Edit and Remove on every row and collecting a 403 reads as a broken app rather than a permission boundary.

**It is not an enforcement point and cannot be.** It travels to a browser, where anyone can edit it. Every route re-checks the same matrix server-side. It is sent from here so the frontend never re-derives the matrix from `role` — a second copy in JavaScript drifts the first time a scope changes, and it drifts silently.

Compare the two examples: the assistant holds `MANAGE_AIRCRAFT` at `READ` (may look, may not change) and `MANAGE_USERS` at `NONE`, where the owner holds `ALL` throughout.

request.description:
Rotates the token pair using the `tj_refresh` cookie.

The old token is revoked and linked to its replacement. **Replaying a revoked token means it leaked**, so every session for that user is revoked rather than just rejecting the one request.

A 30-day "Remember me" session keeps its length across rotation.

item.name: 04 · Password reset
item.description:
Screens `/forgot-password` → `/forgot-password/verify` → `/reset-password`. Run in order; each step unlocks the next via the `tj_pwreset` cookie.

**This folder really changes a password.** It targets the dedicated `reset-demo@tribecajets.com` account so the other folders keep working; `npm run db:seed` restores it.

request.description:
Starts the reset and emails a 6-digit code.

**Always returns 200 and always sets a `tj_pwreset` cookie**, registered address or not. Omitting the cookie for unknown addresses would leak which emails have accounts just as surely as a 404 would.

The cookie binds the flow to this browser, so a code phished onto another device is unusable.

response.name: 200 · Registered address
200 · Unregistered address (identical shape)
400 · Validation failed

request.description:
Re-issues the code and invalidates the previous one. Rate limited to 3 per 15 minutes.

Ordered **before** Verify on purpose: a resend creates a fresh unverified challenge, so running it between Verify and Set new password would reset the flow and the final step would fail.

request.description:
Unlocks the reset step. **Does not change the password** — that is step 04.

On success the challenge is re-stamped with a shorter window (`PASSWORD_RESET_WINDOW_MINUTES`, default 15) to choose the new password.

request.description:
Completes the reset.

Requires a **verified** challenge — posting here without running step 02 fails.

**Revokes every existing session on success.** If the reset happened because the account was compromised, leaving the attacker signed in would defeat the exercise. A notification email is sent to the account holder.

**Password policy:** at least 10 characters with one lowercase, one uppercase and one digit, and different from the current password.

**This is also how an invitation is accepted.** An invited account has no password anyone knows, so setting one here is the act of accepting: a row still in `INVITED` becomes `ACTIVE` in the same transaction, and the user can sign in immediately.

The promotion is deliberately narrow. Only `INVITED` is touched — a `SUSPENDED` account that resets its password stays suspended and still cannot sign in. Status after activation is an administrative decision, and a password reset must never be a way around it. (A suspended account cannot even start a reset: `01 · Request reset code` hands it the same decoy challenge an unknown address gets.)

item.description: Clears every auth cookie and revokes the refresh token server-side. Runs last in this module so the folders above keep their session.

request.description:
Revokes the refresh token server-side and clears every auth cookie. Returns 204 with no body.

Placed near the end of the collection so a top-to-bottom run keeps its session through the Clients folder.

item.name: 03 · Clients
item.description:
Clients and travel agents.

Signed in automatically as the owner by this folder's pre-request script, so it runs standalone. To watch row-level scoping, sign in as `04 · Broker` from the Auth folder and re-run `01 · List clients`: `meta.total` drops to the clients assigned to them.

query.description: Page number, min 1. Default 1.
Rows per page. Integer 1-100. Default 10, matching the rows-per-page dropdown in the UI. Capped so nobody can pull the whole table in one request; >100 or <1 → 400.
Matches first/last name, company, email or phone (case-insensitive).
Allowed (case-sensitive): createdAt | updatedAt | lastName | firstName | leadStage. Default createdAt. A closed list — anything else returns 400 rather than reaching the database.
Allowed (case-sensitive): asc | desc. Default desc.
Allowed (case-sensitive): DIRECT | TRAVEL_AGENT
Allowed (case-sensitive): NEW | CONTACTED | QUOTED | NEGOTIATING | BOOKED | LOST
Allowed (case-sensitive): DIRECT | TRAVEL_AGENT | FACEBOOK_GROUP_1 | FACEBOOK_GROUP_2 | REFERRAL | WEBSITE | OTHER
UUID. Admins only in practice — brokers are already scoped to themselves.
Exact, case-sensitive match against one of the client's labels.

Allowed (case-sensitive): true | false. Default false — only live rows. `true` returns ONLY archived ones, which is what the Archived tab reads. Replaces the old `includeDeleted`, which used a coercion where the string "false" evaluated to true — so asking to exclude removed rows included them.
Filter to one relationship status. Allowed (case-sensitive): LEAD | ACTIVE | VIP | INACTIVE. Omit for all.
Filter by follow-up window, resolved against the current clock. Allowed (case-sensitive): OVERDUE | TODAY | UPCOMING. Omit for all.

request.description:
Paginated list of clients and travel agents.

**Row-level scoping:** a `BROKER` receives only the clients assigned to them, applied inside the SQL `WHERE` clause — so `meta.total` reflects what they can actually see rather than being censored after the fact. Admins see everything.

Response carries `meta` alongside `data` with the pagination cursor fields.

See the Params tab for every filter and its exact allowed values.

**`sortBy` is a closed list.** A column outside it returns 400 rather than falling back to `createdAt` silently — sorting by an unindexed column is a table scan, and accepting the name would confirm which columns exist.

if (err) { console.warn('teardown could not archive ' + id, err); }
* Signs this folder in as the seeded SUPER_ADMIN.
* Runs before every request in the folder but only acts when the
* current session is for a different account, so it costs one login
* per run rather than one per request. `pm.variables` is run-scoped,
* so a fresh run always re-authenticates.
* This is why no folder below `01 · Auth` contains a login request:
* auth endpoints are documented once, in one place.
if (err) { console.error('session setup failed', err); return; }
// security@ has two-factor on, so a password alone leaves the
// session incomplete. Finish the challenge before continuing,
// or every request in the folder 401s.
body: { mode: 'raw', raw: JSON.stringify({ code: code }) },

item.name: 04 · Users
item.description:
Team directory, invitations, role and status administration, and the permission matrix behind the Roles & Permissions tab.

**Two layers of authorization apply.**

1. *Capability* — `Manage Users` is held only by `SUPER_ADMIN` and `ADMIN`. Without it, every write here returns **403**.
2. *Projection* — `GET /users` is open to any signed-in user, because every module needs a staff picker (the client form's Assigned Broker dropdown is the first). Callers without `Manage Users` get a reduced response: names and roles only, no status, no login history, and only `ACTIVE` accounts.

**A row the caller may not see returns 404, never 403.** A 403 would confirm the account exists and turn any id into an existence oracle.

Run `01 · Sign in` first — it captures `csrfToken` for every write below.

pm.test('returns a page with meta', function () {

query.description: Page number. Integer, min 1. Default 1. Out of range → 400.
Rows per page. Integer 1-100. Default 10, matching the rows-per-page dropdown in the UI. Capped so nobody can pull the whole table in one request; >100 or <1 → 400.

Allowed (case-sensitive): createdAt | updatedAt | firstName | lastName | email | role | status | lastLoginAt. Default createdAt. A closed list — anything else returns 400 rather than reaching the database.
Allowed (case-sensitive): asc | desc. Default desc.
Case-insensitive substring match on firstName, lastName or email. Omit for no search.
Allowed (case-sensitive): SUPER_ADMIN | ADMIN | SENIOR_BROKER | BROKER | ASSISTANT. Omit for all roles.
Allowed (case-sensitive): ACTIVE | INVITED | SUSPENDED. Omit for all statuses. Callers without Manage Users always see ACTIVE only, whatever is passed here.

request.description:
Paginated staff directory.

**Response envelope**

```
{ success, data: [...], meta }
```

`meta` carries `page`, `limit`, `total`, `totalPages`, `hasNext`, `hasPrevious`. Paging is entirely server-side — `total` counts what this caller may actually see, not the table size.

**Two different response shapes**, depending on the caller:

- *With* `Manage Users`: full record including `status`, `lastLoginAt`, `twoFactorEnabled`, `phone`, `invitedAt`, `permissionLevel`.
- *Without*: `id`, `email`, `firstName`, `lastName`, `role`, `avatarKey` only — enough to populate a staff picker, nothing more. Compare the two 200 examples.

See the Params tab for every filter and its exact case-sensitive values.

request.description:
Everything the Roles & Permissions tab renders, generated from the server-side matrix — so the table an administrator reads is the ruleset the API actually enforces, not a frontend copy that drifts.

**`roles[]`** — one entry per role with `permissionLevel`, `description`, live `userCount`, `assignable` (false for `SUPER_ADMIN`, which is never offered in the UI), and the role's full permission map.

**`matrix[]`** — one entry per permission with its display `label` and a `scopes` object keyed by role.

**`scopes[]`** — the scope vocabulary, in increasing order of reach:

| Scope | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `NONE` | No access. The guard rejects the request. |
| `READ` | May view, may not modify. |
| `ASSIGNED` | Only rows assigned to this user. |
| `OWN` | Only rows this user owns or originated. |
| `ALL` | Every row. |

Scopes rather than booleans, because the matrix has "Own Only", "Assigned" and "View" cells that a boolean cannot express.

Available to every signed-in user: the frontend hides controls the caller cannot use. That is a courtesy — the guard on each route is the actual enforcement.

No parameters.

request.description:
Creates an account in `INVITED` status.

**How the account activates.** `INVITED` is a pending state, not a disabled one, and nothing an administrator can send will move it. The invitee opens the sign-in page, uses “Forgot password?” with this address, and sets a password — that act *is* accepting the invitation, and the account becomes `ACTIVE` in the same transaction. Until then they cannot sign in, and `06 · Update team member` refuses any status change on the row. To withdraw an invitation, remove the user.

**No password is accepted here, by design.** The account is created with a random, discarded password that is never usable, and the invitee sets a real one through the normal password-reset flow. So a credential is never chosen by, transmitted to, or known by the person doing the inviting.

**Email delivery follows the SMTP config.** With SMTP configured an invitation goes out and `invitation.emailSent` is `true`. Without it, `emailSent` is `false` and `invitation.notice` explains what to tell the invitee instead — rather than failing silently and leaving them waiting for mail that never sent.

Re-inviting a previously removed account revives that row rather than creating a duplicate, so its audit history stays attached.

Requires `Manage Users`.

body.raw:
{
  "email": "{{inviteEmail}}",  // required · valid email, stored lowercase. This is the login identity and cannot be changed later. Already in use by a live account → 409.

  "firstName": "Avery",        // required · 1-100 chars

  "lastName": "Newman",        // required · 1-100 chars

  "phone": "+1 555 0163",      // optional · max 40 chars, free-form

  "role": "BROKER"             // optional · default "BROKER" · Allowed (case-sensitive): "ADMIN" | "SENIOR_BROKER" | "BROKER" | "ASSISTANT" "SUPER_ADMIN" is deliberately NOT assignable: it would let an admin mint an account immune to their own administration.
}

variable.description: UUID of the team member to update. Populated by `06 · Invite team member`, so running this folder in order never mutates a seeded account.

request.description:
Partial update. Send only the fields you are changing; at least one is required (an empty body returns 400).

**Deliberately absent:** `email` (the login identity and the anchor of the audit trail) and `password` (never set by an administrator).

### Status is `ACTIVE` or `SUSPENDED` — never `INVITED`

`INVITED` is not a decision anyone makes. An account is created in it by `05 · Invite team member` and leaves it exactly once, on its own, when the invitee sets a password through `01 · Auth / 04 · Password reset`. Two rules follow, and both are enforced:

| Attempt | Result |
|---|---|
| Send `"status": "INVITED"` | 400 — the enum accepts only `ACTIVE` and `SUSPENDED` |
| Send any status for an account still in `INVITED` | 400 — withdraw the invitation with `07 · Remove team member` instead |

Suspending a pending invitation would strand the row: the invitee cannot sign in, and completing the reset would no longer activate them, so nothing could move the account again.

Once the account is `ACTIVE`, suspending and reactivating it is an ordinary administrative decision — and a password reset never undoes it. A suspended user who resets their password stays suspended.

### Refusals that protect the system from its own administrators

| Attempt | Result |
|---|---|
| Change your own role | 400 |
| Set your own status to anything but `ACTIVE` | 400 |
| Modify the `SUPER_ADMIN` owner (unless you are it) | 403 |
| Demote or suspend the last active administrator | 400 |

The last-administrator check counts against the live database rather than the request, because two admins demoting each other concurrently would each individually look safe.

Role and status changes are written to the audit log as `user.access_changed` with before/after values.

Requires `Manage Users`.

item.name: 05 · Airports
item.description:
Airports are **shared reference data**: every signed-in caller sees the same rows, because unlike a client, nobody owns an airport. There is no row-level scoping here — only whether you may edit the master list.

### Who may write

| Role | Read | Create / Edit / Remove |
|---|---|---|
| SUPER_ADMIN, ADMIN, SENIOR_BROKER | ✓ | ✓ |
| BROKER, ASSISTANT | ✓ | 403 |

Brokers and assistants hold `MANAGE_AIRPORTS` at **READ** scope. They must be able to read the table — a broker cannot build a trip without picking an airport — but an airport is an objective fact about the world, not desk opinion, and a wrong runway length silently makes a trip unbookable.

This folder runs as the seeded owner.

query.description: Page number, 1-based. Integer ≥1. Default 1. Out of range returns an empty `data` with a truthful `meta`.
Rows per page. Integer 1-100. Default 10, matching the rows-per-page dropdown in the UI. >100 or <1 → 400.
Case-insensitive substring. Trimmed, max 200 chars.
Allowed (case-sensitive): asc | desc. Default desc — tables open newest-first.
Exact match on the stored country string, case-sensitive (`USA`, not `usa`). Options come from `03 · Countries`. Omit for all countries.

Allowed (case-sensitive): createdAt | updatedAt | icao | iata | name | city | country | longestRunwayFt. Default createdAt, paired with sortOrder desc, so a newly added airport is the first row. A closed list — anything else returns 400 rather than reaching the database.

Allowed (case-sensitive): true | false. Default false — only live rows. `true` returns ONLY archived ones, which is what the Archived tab reads. One endpoint serves both halves of the table; a separate /archived route would duplicate every filter and sort param and the two would drift.

request.description:
Paginated list. Search covers **ICAO, IATA, name, city and country** in one term.

`latitude` and `longitude` come back as JSON numbers, not the `{s,e,d}` shape a raw Prisma Decimal would serialise to.

See the Params tab for every filter, its default and its bounds.

`domestic` counts rows whose country equals `homeCountry`, and `international` is the remainder. `homeCountry` is returned explicitly rather than assumed by the UI, because "domestic" is meaningless without saying relative to where.

request.description:
Creates an airport. Requires `Manage Airports` at write scope — brokers and assistants receive 403.

**ICAO is normalised and unique.** It is upper-cased on the way in, so `kteb` and `KTEB` are the same airport and cannot both exist.

**Adding a removed airport restores it** rather than returning 409. A soft delete keeps the code occupied, so refusing would strand the caller: they can see no KBED in the list and cannot create one either. The revived row keeps its original audit history instead of starting a second record for the same physical airport, and the audit entry reads `airport.restored`. The 409 below is for a code held by a **live** airport.

header.description: Required on every write. Captured automatically after any login or refresh.

variable.description: UUID of the archived airport, from `05 · Add airport`.

request.description:
Brings an archived airport back **exactly as it was** — clears the deletion stamp and touches nothing else.

This is the only way to restore. `05 · Add airport` refuses an archived ICAO rather than reviving it, because re-running a create form would overwrite eleven stored fields with whatever was typed into it.

No conflict check is needed: ICAO is unique across live *and* archived rows, so nothing can have taken the code while this row held it.

A row that is not archived returns 404 — restoring something that was never removed is meaningless, and a 403 would confirm the id exists.

request.description:
Removes every id in one statement, for the table's checkbox column.

**POST, not DELETE.** Request bodies on DELETE are unevenly supported by proxies and HTTP clients; a silently dropped body would remove nothing and still answer 200.

**Partial success is success.** Ids matching nothing — already removed, or never there — come back in `skipped` rather than failing the batch. Two people clearing the same rows is ordinary, and refusing the second one would make their click do nothing at all.

Soft delete, like `07`: re-adding an ICAO restores that airport.

item.name: 06 · Operators
item.description:
Charter operators — the companies that actually fly the aircraft. **Shared master data**, the same rows for every signed-in caller, with no row-level scoping.

### Who may write

| Role | Read | Create / Edit / Remove |
|---|---|---|
| SUPER_ADMIN, ADMIN, SENIOR_BROKER, BROKER | ✓ | ✓ |
| ASSISTANT | ✓ | 403 |

Brokers may write here but not in `05 · Airports`: a broker who sources a new operator adds it themselves, which matches the `Operator Sourcing` permission they already hold at full scope. Assistants hold `MANAGE_OPERATORS` at **READ**.

### Fields the UI shows that nothing can supply yet

`totalTrips`, `totalPaid` and `totalFleet` are aggregates over trips, operator payments and aircraft — none of which exist. They return **null**, not 0, so the UI can render an honest em dash: a confident "0 trips" against an operator the desk has flown twice is a wrong answer. Same reason `fleet`, `tripHistory` and `payments` come back as empty arrays on the detail response.

This folder runs as the seeded owner.

query.description: Page number, 1-based. Integer ≥1. Default 1. Out of range returns an empty `data` with a truthful `meta`.
Rows per page. Integer 1-100. Default 10, matching the rows-per-page dropdown in the UI. >100 or <1 → 400.
Case-insensitive substring. Trimmed, max 200 chars.
Allowed (case-sensitive): asc | desc. Default desc — tables open newest-first.
Allowed (case-sensitive): ACTIVE | PREFERRED | INACTIVE. Omit for all statuses. Lower-case returns 400 rather than being silently corrected.

Allowed (case-sensitive): createdAt | updatedAt | name | status | reliabilityRating. Default createdAt, paired with sortOrder desc, so a newly added operator is the first row. A closed list — anything else returns 400 rather than reaching the database.
Allowed (case-sensitive): true | false. Default false — only live rows. `true` returns ONLY archived ones, for the Archived tab.

exec: // Teardown. This is the last request in the folder, and the folder ends
// by restoring the operator it created — so every run used to leave
// one more live operator behind. Thirty-seven had piled up in
// There is no hard delete in this system by design, so the run cannot
// erase its own row. Archiving it is the best available end state: the
// debris sits in the Archived tab instead of among the records the desk
if (err) { console.warn('teardown could not archive ' + id, err); }
* Signs this folder in as the seeded SUPER_ADMIN.
* Runs before every request in the folder but only acts when the
* current session is for a different account, so it costs one login
* per run rather than one per request. `pm.variables` is run-scoped,
* so a fresh run always re-authenticates.
* This is why no folder below `01 · Auth` contains a login request:
* auth endpoints are documented once, in one place.
if (err) { console.error('session setup failed', err); return; }
// security@ has two-factor on, so a password alone leaves the
// session incomplete. Finish the challenge before continuing,
// or every request in the folder 401s.
body: { mode: 'raw', raw: JSON.stringify({ code: code }) },
// Writes need X-CSRF-Token, and the value is only readable from the
// Parsed out of Set-Cookie rather than read from pm.cookies.jar():
// the jar is not reliably populated in Newman, and a jar read that
// comes back empty would clobber a working token with undefined.

item.name: 07 · Aircraft
item.description:
The fleet: individual airframes, each belonging to an operator and usually based at an airport.

Both of those are real foreign keys, which is why Operators and Airports had to ship first — see AGENTS.md on build order. Quotes, trips, empty legs and flight tracking will all reference this table.

Every request below is signed in as the seeded SUPER_ADMIN by the folder's pre-request script, except the 403 examples, which were captured as the seeded assistant.

query.description: Page number, 1-based. Integer ≥1. Default 1. Out of range returns an empty `data` with a truthful `meta`.
Rows per page. Integer 1-100. Default 10, matching the rows-per-page dropdown in the UI. >100 or <1 → 400.
Case-insensitive substring across tail number, model, manufacturer, the operator's name and the home base's ICAO, name and city. Trimmed, max 200 chars.
Allowed (case-sensitive): asc | desc. Default desc — tables open newest-first.

Allowed (case-sensitive): createdAt | updatedAt | tailNumber | model | category | status | maxPassengers | rangeNm | yearBuilt. Default createdAt, paired with sortOrder desc, so a newly added tail is the first row. A closed list — anything else returns 400 rather than reaching the database.
Allowed (case-sensitive): AVAILABLE | IN_SERVICE | MAINTENANCE | INACTIVE. Omit for all. Lower-case returns 400 rather than being silently corrected.
Allowed (case-sensitive): TURBOPROP | LIGHT_JET | MIDSIZE_JET | SUPER_MIDSIZE | HEAVY_JET | ULTRA_LONG_RANGE | VIP_AIRLINER. Omit for all.
uuid. Only this operator's fleet — what the operator detail page's Fleet tab reads.
uuid. Only aircraft based at this airport.
The fleet finder (scope §6.8). Integer 1-200. Seats AT LEAST this many — more seats still answers "what can carry nine". A tail with no capacity recorded is excluded, not assumed to fit.
Integer 1-20000 nautical miles, AT LEAST. Same rule: an unknown range is excluded rather than guessed.

Cabin-preference filtering (scope §6.8). Comma separated ("WiFi,Full Galley"), max 400 chars. The aircraft must have ALL of them — a requested feature is a requirement, so one missing makes it a wrong answer, not a weaker match. Values come from GET /aircraft/amenities and are matched exactly, including case.
Allowed (case-sensitive): true | false. Default false — only live rows. `true` returns ONLY archived ones, for the Archived tab.

request.description:
Paginated list of the fleet. Search covers **tail number, model, manufacturer, the operator's name and the home base's ICAO, name and city** in one term — "VistaJet" and "Aspen" both find aircraft, even though neither is a column on this table.

`operator` and `homeBase` come back as objects rather than names, so the table can link to them and cannot show a stale name after a rename.

`totalTrips`, `tripsThisYear` and `avgUtilization` are **null**, not 0: they are aggregates over trips, and that module does not exist yet. Null lets the UI show an em dash instead of claiming a tail has never flown.

See the Params tab for every filter, its default and its bounds.

request.description:
Every cabin feature recorded on a live aircraft, de-duplicated and sorted — the options for the preference filter.

Derived from the rows rather than a list fixed at design time, so the dropdown can never offer a feature nothing matches or omit one somebody typed yesterday. De-duplicated **case-insensitively**: "WiFi" and "Wifi" are one preference typed twice, and offering both would split the fleet for no reason.

Feed these values back to `GET /aircraft?amenities=` exactly as returned — the filter matches case.

request.description:
Adds an aircraft. Requires `Manage Aircraft` at write scope — assistants receive 403; brokers may add, matching how they may add an operator.

**Only tail number, model and category are required.** A tail is usually catalogued from a sourcing call with little more than the model, and demanding a full specification sheet up front only produces invented numbers.

**The tail number is normalised and unique.** It is upper-cased on the way in, so `n780ex` and `N780EX` are the same airframe and cannot both exist. Unlike an airport ICAO, a tail held by an **archived** aircraft is *not* silently revived — the 409 names the situation and points at `08 · Restore aircraft`, because an archived tail is usually a real airframe someone wants back with its history, not a code to recycle.

**`operatorId` and `homeBaseId` are checked, not just constrained.** An unknown id returns a named 400 rather than a bare foreign-key error, and an *archived* operator is refused — the row still exists, so the database constraint alone would accept it.

request.description:
Partial update — send only what changed. An empty body returns 400 rather than a no-op 200, so a broken client is visible instead of silent.

Archived aircraft return 404: restore first, then edit.

A row that is not archived returns 404 — restoring a live aircraft is not a no-op, it is a sign the caller has the wrong id.

item.name: 08 · Trip Requests
item.description:
Open trip requests — what a client asked for, before it becomes a quote or a trip (scope §6.4).

**This is the other half of a lead.** A lead is a *person*: a Client at lead stage, in `03 · Clients`. What they asked for is one of these. They are two records because one client can ask for three different trips, and because the request outlives the lead stage while the client stays a client.

Uses the **trips** permissions rather than a new pair, because a request is the start of a trip: `VIEW_TRIPS` to read, `MANAGE_TRIPS` to write, `DELETE_TRIPS` (administrators only) to archive.

Every request below is signed in as the seeded SUPER_ADMIN by the folder's pre-request script, except the 403 examples, captured as the seeded broker and assistant.

query.description: Page number, 1-based. Integer ≥1. Default 1.
Rows per page. Integer 1-100. Default 10. >100 or <1 → 400.
Case-insensitive substring across the summary, the client's name and company, and both airports' ICAO codes.
Allowed (case-sensitive): asc | desc. Default desc.
Allowed (case-sensitive): createdAt | updatedAt | departureDate | status | estimatedValue | passengers. Default createdAt. A closed list — anything else returns 400.
Allowed: true | false. Default false. `true` hides CONVERTED and LOST — the working board is a list of things still needing a price, and finished requests bury them.
Allowed (case-sensitive): OPEN | SOURCING | QUOTED | CONVERTED | LOST. Lower-case returns 400 rather than being silently corrected.
Allowed (case-sensitive): DIRECT | TRAVEL_AGENT | FACEBOOK_GROUP_1 | FACEBOOK_GROUP_2 | REFERRAL | WEBSITE | OTHER.
Allowed (case-sensitive): TURBOPROP | LIGHT_JET | MIDSIZE_JET | SUPER_MIDSIZE | HEAVY_JET | ULTRA_LONG_RANGE | VIP_AIRLINER.
uuid. One client's enquiries — what the lead detail page reads.
uuid.
uuid.
uuid.
Allowed (case-sensitive): OVERDUE | TODAY | UPCOMING. Departure relative to today.
Allowed: true | false. Default false — live rows only. `true` returns ONLY archived ones.

request.description:
Open trip requests — the enquiry, before it becomes a quote or a trip (scope §6.4).

**Scoped.** A broker sees the enquiries assigned to them *plus any not yet assigned to anyone* — an unowned request is exactly the one that must not disappear. Applied in the query, so their pagination counts and pipeline totals are correct rather than merely censored.

`client`, `assignedBroker` and both airports come back as objects rather than names, so the board can link to them and cannot show a stale name after a rename.

Use `openOnly=true` for the working board.

header.description: Required on every write. Captured automatically after any login or refresh.

body.raw:
{
  "clientId": "{{clientId}}",                          // required · uuid of a live client. The ONLY required field — an enquiry with nobody attached cannot be followed up, quoted or converted. For a travel agent's enquiry this is the agent, who is a client of type TRAVEL_AGENT.

  "source": "REFERRAL",                                // optional · DIRECT | TRAVEL_AGENT | FACEBOOK_GROUP_1 | FACEBOOK_GROUP_2 | REFERRAL | WEBSITE | OTHER. Default DIRECT. Same enum the client's leadSource uses — one vocabulary, not two.
  "status": "OPEN",                                    // optional · OPEN | SOURCING | QUOTED | CONVERTED | LOST. Default OPEN.

  "assignedBrokerId": "{{userId}}",                    // optional · uuid. A BROKER always files against themselves, whatever is sent here; assigning to someone else needs a wider scope.

  "originAirportId": "{{airportId}}",                  // optional · uuid of a live airport  // Route. Real airport ids, not codes typed into a box.
  "destinationAirportId": null,                        // optional · uuid, or null

  "departureDate": "2026-11-15",                       // optional                           // YYYY-MM-DD, no time of day. A present returnDate is what makes this a round trip — there is no separate flag, because two fields that can disagree will. A return before the departure returns 400.
  "returnDate": "2026-11-18",                          // optional

  "passengers": 4,                                     // optional · integer 1-200. An empty string is stored as absent, never as 0.
  "aircraftPreference": "HEAVY_JET",                   // optional · TURBOPROP | LIGHT_JET | MIDSIZE_JET | SUPER_MIDSIZE | HEAVY_JET | ULTRA_LONG_RANGE | VIP_AIRLINER. A category, not a tail — at enquiry stage nobody has picked an airframe.
  "estimatedValue": 28000,                             // optional · number 0-100000000, whole currency units. Feeds the pipeline total, so it is DECIMAL not float.

  "summary": "NYC → Miami, business charter",          // optional · max 300 chars. One line for the board's Route column.
  "requirements": "Catering and ground transport.",    // optional · max 2000 chars. What the client asked for.
  "internalNotes": "Referred by Hope Sterling."        // optional · max 2000 chars. Never shown to a client.
}

request.description:
Files an enquiry. This is the second half of the Add Lead form: a lead is a *person* (a Client at lead stage) and what they asked for is this record, because one client can ask for three different trips and because the request outlives the lead stage — it becomes a quote, then a trip, while the client stays a client.

**Only `clientId` is required.** Everything else can arrive later; demanding a full route on a first phone call only produces guesses.

A **broker files against themselves** whatever `assignedBrokerId` says — assigning to someone else needs a wider scope.

exec: // Teardown. This is the last request in the folder and leaves the
// enquiry it created LIVE, so every run would add a probe to the
// working board. There is no hard delete by design, so archiving it
// is the best available end state: debris sits in the Archived tab
// rather than among the requests a broker is trying to price.
if (err) { console.warn('teardown could not archive ' + id, err); }
* Signs this folder in as the seeded SUPER_ADMIN.
* Runs before every request in the folder but only acts when the
* current session is for a different account, so it costs one login
* per run rather than one per request. `pm.variables` is run-scoped,
* so a fresh run always re-authenticates.
* This is why no folder below `01 · Auth` contains a login request:
* auth endpoints are documented once, in one place.
if (err) { console.error('session setup failed', err); return; }
// security@ has two-factor on, so a password alone leaves the
// session incomplete. Finish the challenge before continuing,
// or every request in the folder 401s.
body: { mode: 'raw', raw: JSON.stringify({ code: code }) },
// Writes need X-CSRF-Token, and the value is only readable from the
// Parsed out of Set-Cookie rather than read from pm.cookies.jar():
// the jar is not reliably populated in Newman, and a jar read that
// comes back empty would clobber a working token with undefined.

item.name: 09 · Operator Sourcing
item.description:
Asking operators to price an enquiry, and comparing what comes back (scope §6.7 and §6.9).

**One new table, not two.** The sourcing board's rows are trip requests being worked — the same record the Open Requests board shows — so the only genuinely new entity here is the operator's answer. A second requests table would have split one enquiry across two rows the way a leads table would have split one client.

Uses the **trips** permissions rather than its own pair: sourcing is a stage of a trip, not something a role is granted separately. `VIEW_TRIPS` to read, `MANAGE_TRIPS` to write, `DELETE_TRIPS` (administrators only) to archive.

Every request below is signed in as the seeded SUPER_ADMIN by the folder's pre-request script, except the 403 examples, which were captured as the seeded assistant and broker.

query.description: Page number, 1-based. Integer ≥1. Default 1.
Rows per page. Integer 1-100. Default 10. >100 or <1 → 400.
Case-insensitive substring across the operator's name, the quoted aircraft and tail, and the linked tail's number and model.
Allowed (case-sensitive): asc | desc. Default desc.
Allowed (case-sensitive): createdAt | updatedAt | requestedAt | respondedAt | price | status. Default createdAt. A closed list — anything else returns 400.
uuid. Every quote on one enquiry — how the comparison view loads.
uuid. One operator's quote history, which is what their scorecard is counted from.
uuid. Only matches quotes that named a tail we hold.
Allowed (case-sensitive): AWAITING_RESPONSE | RECEIVED | APPROVED | REJECTED | DECLINED. Lower-case returns 400 rather than being silently corrected.
Allowed: true | false. Default false. `true` keeps only AWAITING_RESPONSE and RECEIVED — the ones still needing something from somebody.
Allowed: true | false. Default false — live rows only. `true` returns ONLY archived ones.

request.description:
Operator sourcing — what each operator came back with on an enquiry (scope §6.7 and §6.9).

**Sourcing adds one table, not two.** The board's rows are trip requests being worked: client, broker, route, departure and budget are all TripRequest columns, and the New Sourcing Request form is the trip-request form with a quote deadline added. The only genuinely new record is this one.

**Scoped through the enquiry.** A broker sees quotes on the requests assigned to them plus any unassigned. Doing it through the relation rather than copying `assignedBrokerId` onto the quote means reassigning a request moves its quotes with it, with no backfill.

**Two fields are computed on every read and never stored**: `responseHours`, measured from the ask to the answer, and `isOverdue`, the enquiry's quote deadline against today. A stored "2h" is right for one day and wrong forever after, and the operator scorecard is built on response speed.

exec: // The requests below need a real quote, an enquiry and an operator.

request.description:
Counts by state plus the average response time, scoped like the list so a broker's tiles always agree with the rows underneath them.

`averageResponseHours` is **null, never 0**, when nothing has been answered yet. A desk that has just started sourcing has no response time, and 0 would read as every operator replying instantly.

response.name: 200 · Tiles

request.description:
Archived quotes load here too, because the Archived tab links straight to them.

A quote outside the caller’s scope returns **404, not 403** — a 403 confirms the record exists and turns any id into an oracle.

body.raw:
{
  "tripRequestId": "{{tripRequestId}}",                // required · uuid of a live trip request you can see. Sourcing hangs off an enquiry — there is no free-standing quote.
  "operatorId": "{{operatorId}}",                      // required · uuid of a live operator. An archived one returns 400 saying so, rather than "does not exist".

  "suggestedAircraft": "Challenger 650 or similar",    // optional · max 200 chars. What WE asked for, in the broker's words. Free text on purpose: the ask describes a mission, not one airframe we already hold.

  "aircraftId": null,                                  // optional · uuid, or null                                                                                                                                                                            // What they offered. Two fields, deliberately: aircraftId is the real tail when it is one we hold — and it must be on THIS operator's certificate, or 400 — and the text fields carry what the operator wrote when it is not. Operators fly tails we have never entered; refusing the quote over that would lose the quote.
  "quotedAircraft": "Challenger 650",                  // optional · max 200 chars
  "quotedTailNumber": "N650XY",                        // optional · max 12 chars

  "price": 29850,                                      // optional · number 0-100000000, whole currency units, USD. DECIMAL not float — money does not round in binary. 0 is a real quote (a waived positioning leg), which is why the floor is 0 and not 1.  // A price may be sent with the ask. A broker who got the number on the call would otherwise have to record a response a second later, logging a response time of zero for a quote that took a day. Sent with a price, the quote starts at RECEIVED; without one, at AWAITING_RESPONSE.

  "amenities": ["WiFi", "Full Galley"],                // optional · up to 30 chips, each 1-60 chars. Same vocabulary as Aircraft.amenities so the comparison view reads one list. Replaced wholesale on update, never merged.
  "terms": "Net 30. 50% fee within 48 hours.",         // optional · max 2000 chars. Free text: every operator words these differently, and parsing them into columns is what scope §18 warns breaks.

  "internalNotes": "Called Dana directly."             // optional · max 2000 chars. Never shown to a client or an operator.
}

request.description:
Creates the ask and moves the enquiry to **SOURCING**.

**One live ask per operator per enquiry.** Asking the same operator twice is a mistake, not a second quote, and the comparison view would show them twice — the duplicate returns 409. Enforced in the service so the message explains itself, and by a partial unique index in Postgres so it still holds when two brokers send the same ask at the same moment.

A price may be sent with the ask: sent with one the quote starts at RECEIVED, without one at AWAITING_RESPONSE.

exec: // Teardown. This is the last request in the folder, and the folder ends
// by restoring the quote it created — so every run would otherwise leave
// one more live quote on the sourcing board. Clients, airports and
// operators each accumulated dozens that way before anyone noticed.
// There is no hard delete in this system by design, so the run cannot
// erase its own row. Archiving it is the best available end state.
if (err) { console.warn('teardown could not archive ' + id, err); }
* Signs this folder in as the seeded SUPER_ADMIN.
* Runs before every request in the folder but only acts when the
* current session is for a different account, so it costs one login
* per run rather than one per request. `pm.variables` is run-scoped,
* so a fresh run always re-authenticates.
* This is why no folder below `01 · Auth` contains a login request:
* auth endpoints are documented once, in one place.
if (err) { console.error('session setup failed', err); return; }
// security@ has two-factor on, so a password alone leaves the
// session incomplete. Finish the challenge before continuing,
// or every request in the folder 401s.
body: { mode: 'raw', raw: JSON.stringify({ code: code }) },
// Writes need X-CSRF-Token, and the value is only readable from the
// Parsed out of Set-Cookie rather than read from pm.cookies.jar():
// the jar is not reliably populated in Newman, and a jar read that
// comes back empty would clobber a working token with undefined.

item.name: 10 · Quotes
item.description:
The client-facing offer: what Tribeca Jets sells the flight for, with margin and Federal Excise Tax on top of what the operator charges (scope §6.10).

**Two quote entities, deliberately.** §10 of the scope lists Operator Quote and Client Quote separately, and they are different records: one is what an operator charges us (folder 09), the other is what the client pays. Approving an operator’s price does not create the client’s offer — the desk decides the markup — so `operatorQuoteId` links them without making one the other.

**Nothing computed is stored.** `fetAmount`, `extrasTotal`, `totalPrice`, `grossProfit` and `marginPercentage` are worked out on every read from the four inputs a person actually typed. The one place frozen figures are needed — "what exactly did the client see on the 9th?" — is the version history in request 04, which snapshots the whole set each time the money moves.

Uses the **trips** permissions, like trip requests and sourcing: a quote is a stage of a trip, not a capability a role is granted on its own. `VIEW_TRIPS` to read, `MANAGE_TRIPS` to write, `DELETE_TRIPS` (administrators only) to archive. The **margin** carries a second gate, `VIEW_FINANCIALS`, which an assistant does not hold.

Every request below is signed in as the seeded SUPER_ADMIN by the folder’s pre-request script, except the 403 examples and the assistant’s read, captured as the seeded assistant and broker.

query.description: Page number, 1-based. Integer ≥1. Default 1.
Rows per page. Integer 1-100. Default 10. >100 or <1 → 400.
Case-insensitive substring across the client's name and company, the operator's name, the quoted aircraft and tail, and both airport ICAO codes.
Allowed (case-sensitive): asc | desc. Default desc.

Allowed (case-sensitive): createdAt | updatedAt | reference | basePrice | status | departureDate | validUntil | sentAt. Default createdAt — newest first, so a quote just written is the first thing you see. A closed list: anything else returns 400.
Allowed (case-sensitive): DRAFT | SENT | VIEWED | APPROVED | REJECTED | EXPIRED. Lower-case returns 400 rather than being silently corrected.
uuid. Every quote for one client — how the client detail page's Quotes tab loads.
uuid. One broker’s quotes, which their conversion rate is counted from.
uuid. Every offer built from one enquiry. An enquiry can be quoted more than once — a different aircraft, a different operator — and the desk compares them.
uuid. Quotes naming this operator as the one flying it.
Allowed: true | false. Default false. `true` keeps only DRAFT, SENT and VIEWED — the ones still waiting on the client. A month of approved quotes buries the one expiring on Friday.

Allowed: true | false. Default false. `true` keeps only live offers whose validUntil has passed. Asks the database the same date question the `isExpired` badge asks on read, so the filter and the badge can never disagree.
Allowed: true | false. Default false — live rows only. `true` returns ONLY archived ones.

request.description:
Client quotes — the offer the client is shown, with margin and Federal Excise Tax on top of what the operator charges (scope §6.10).

**Two quote tables, deliberately.** An `OperatorQuote` (folder 09) is what an operator charges *us*; a `Quote` is what the client pays. One does not become the other automatically, because the markup is the desk’s decision — which is why `operatorQuoteId` is a link rather than an identity.

**Every money figure below the inputs is computed on read and never stored.** `fetAmount`, `extrasTotal`, `totalPrice`, `grossProfit` and `marginPercentage` are worked out from `basePrice`, `fetRate`, `operatorCost` and `lineItems` on every request. A stored total beside its own parts is the classic accounting bug: the day an edit moves the base price and the total does not follow, the quote contradicts itself and nothing on screen says which half is right.

**`operatorCost`, `grossProfit` and `marginPercentage` are absent entirely** for a caller without `VIEW_FINANCIALS` — an assistant sees the offer and not the desk’s margin. Absent, not zeroed: a `0` margin is a number someone could repeat down the phone.

request.description:
Counts per status, the total value of the quotes in scope, and the average margin — scoped exactly like the list, so a broker’s tiles always agree with the rows underneath them.

**Counted in JavaScript rather than summed in SQL, deliberately.** A quote’s total is derived from its parts, so there is no `totalPrice` column for the database to add up; summing `basePrice` instead would report a figure that is neither the offer nor the revenue, because it leaves out the tax and every extra.

`averageMargin` is **null, never 0**, when nothing has an operator cost against it yet — "we make nothing" and "we have not priced the cost side" are different statements. It is also null for a caller without `VIEW_FINANCIALS`.

request.description:
Every revision of the offer, newest first (scope §6.10, and one of the advanced requirements named in §5).

The question this answers is not "what does this quote say" — the quote itself says that — but **"what exactly did the client see on the 9th, and what changed after?"** So every figure here was written out at the time and **nothing is recomputed**: a snapshot that recalculates from today’s tax rate is not a snapshot.

Append-only. Nothing updates a version and nothing removes one, which is why this is the one model in the system with no archive trail — a record that is never deleted needs no soft delete.

response.name: 200 · Two versions
200 · A quote that has never been revised

header.description: Required on every write. Captured automatically after any login or refresh.

body.raw:
{
  "clientId": "{{clientId}}",                          // required · uuid of a live client. A quote is a financial offer made to a named person; it has to stay attached to one.

  "tripRequestId": "{{tripRequestId}}",                // optional · uuid. The enquiry this answers. Sending the quote moves that enquiry to QUOTED.          // Where the offer came from. Both optional, and both worth sending.
  "operatorQuoteId": "{{operatorQuoteId}}",            // optional · uuid of an OperatorQuote (module 09). This is the seam between the two: an operator quote is what an operator charges US, this is what the client pays. Linking them is what makes the margin traceable to a real number rather than one retyped from another screen.

  "assignedBrokerId": null,                            // optional · uuid, or null. Defaults to the caller ONLY when nobody is named — an admin writing a quote on a broker's behalf must not have it reassigned to themselves.

  "operatorId": "{{operatorId}}",                      // optional · uuid. Who is flying it.

  "aircraftId": null,                                  // optional · uuid, or null                                                                            // The aircraft, two ways — the same pattern operator quotes use. A real tail when it is one we hold, free text when the operator is flying something we have never entered.
  "quotedAircraft": "Gulfstream G550",                 // optional · max 200 chars

  "originAirportId": "{{airportId}}",                  // optional · uuid of a live airport. A real relation, never an ICAO string typed into a box.
  "destinationAirportId": "{{airportId2}}",            // optional · uuid

  "departureDate": "2026-11-14",                       // optional · YYYY-MM-DD. A DAY, not a moment: storing midnight UTC in a timestamp makes it render as the day before west of Greenwich.
  "returnDate": "2026-11-17",                          // optional · YYYY-MM-DD. A present returnDate is what makes it a round trip — there is no separate flag, because two fields that can disagree will.
  "validUntil": "2026-10-20",                          // optional · YYYY-MM-DD. The offer's shelf life. `isExpired` is derived from it on every read, never stored.

  "passengers": 4,                                     // optional · integer 1-100

  "basePrice": 79500,                                  // required · number 0-100000000, whole currency units, USD. The charter price BEFORE tax and extras.  // ---- The priced inputs. Everything else is worked out on read. ----------

  "fetEnabled": true,                                  // optional · boolean, default true. US Federal Excise Tax on domestic air transportation. Set false for an international leg, which is exempt.
  "fetRate": 0.075,                                    // optional · number 0-1. A RATE, not a percentage: 0.075, never 7.5. Above 1 is refused as a typo — "7.5" would turn a $79,500 quote into a $676,000 one, and it would go out to a client. Stored per quote because a statutory rate is a fact about when the quote was written.

  "operatorCost": 65000,                               // optional · number 0-100000000. What the flight costs US. Null until the operator's number is in — a margin of "we do not know yet" must read as unknown, never as 100% profit.
  "depositAmount": 20000,                              // optional · number 0-100000000. What the client pays up front to hold the aircraft.

  "lineItems": [                                       // optional · up to 40 entries                                                                         // Extras on the offer. Each needs either a price or `included: true` — a line with neither has nothing to say, and returns 400.
    { "label": "Catering (seafood premium)", "amount": null, "included": true },
    { "label": "Ground transportation", "amount": 850, "included": false }
  ],

  "terms": "50% on acceptance, balance 72 hours before departure.",   // optional · max 5000 chars. Printed on the quote. CLIENT-FACING.
  "internalNotes": "Client always books the same cabin."              // optional · max 2000 chars. NEVER shown to a client.
}

request.description:
Always created as a **DRAFT at version 1** — nothing reaches a client by being saved, and `status` is not accepted here at all.

**FET is charged on the base charter price only.** US Federal Excise Tax applies to amounts paid for taxable air transportation, which is the charter itself; catering and ground transportation are not that. Charging it across the extras too would overstate the tax on every quote with catering on it, and the client pays that difference.

`fetRate` is a **rate, not a percentage**: 0.075. Anything above 1 is refused, because "7.5" typed meaning 7.5% turns a $79,500 quote into a $676,000 one — and that one would go out.

request.description:
Marks the quote **SENT**, stamps the date the client’s decision window runs from, and moves the enquiry behind it to **QUOTED** — forward only, and never over a request already converted or lost.

**No email is sent.** Nothing in this system delivers to a client yet; that arrives with Email Templates (#21). Pretending otherwise would mean a broker believing a quote had been delivered when it had not.

`sentAt` is stamped on every send, not only the first: a revised quote that goes out again genuinely went out again. The earlier sends are not lost — each one has its version in the log.

request.description:
**Only one quote per enquiry can be approved.** A second attempt returns 409 naming the one already accepted, rather than silently demoting it — two approved quotes on one enquiry mean two aircraft booked for one flight, and the fix has to be a deliberate act: reopen the wrong one, then approve the right one.

A **draft** cannot be approved: nobody has seen it, so there is nothing to agree to.

An **expired** quote can be. The desk choosing to honour a lapsed price is a real decision, and it stays visible because the validity date is still on the row.

item.name: 11 · Uploads
item.description:
One upload surface for the whole product.

A screen posts a file here, gets back a **URL**, and stores that URL on whatever record it is editing — `photoUrl` on an aircraft, an attachment on a referral, a document on a user. Nothing in this folder knows or cares what a file is *for*; that is the business of the record holding the URL.

**Why it works this way.** The upload does not need to know what the file will be attached to, so a photograph can be chosen on a *create* form — before the record it belongs to exists. An API that wanted the aircraft id at upload time could not do that, and every create form would have to save first and upload second, leaving a record with no picture whenever the second call failed.

**Two routes, because there are two kinds of file.** `image` and `document` describe what a file *is*. A *purpose* — "tax form", "id proof", "brochure" — is not a kind, and making it one would put every new upload button in the product behind a migration.

| Route | Accepts | Limit | Folder |
|---|---|---|---|
| `POST /uploads/image` | `image/jpeg | image/png | image/webp | image/gif` | 15 MB | `images/` |
| `POST /uploads/document` | `application/pdf | application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.wordprocessingml.document (.docx) | application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet (.xlsx) | text/plain | text/csv` | 25 MB | `documents/` |

**The content type is read from the bytes, never from the upload header.** A multipart part's `Content-Type` is chosen by whoever sent it, so believing it would let them decide what a browser is later handed — `text/html` served from this API's own origin, with the session cookie attached. Renaming a `.exe` to `.png` changes nothing.

Three formats are refused on purpose. **SVG** is a document that executes script. **Archives** carry their contents past whatever checked the outer file. **Legacy `.doc`/`.xls`** are both OLE2 and byte-identical at the header, so telling them apart would mean trusting the sender.

**Re-uploading a file returns the one already on file.** Deduplication is by SHA-256 of the bytes, scoped to the uploader: the same file sent twice answers `deduplicated: true` with the original `id` and `createdAt`, and writes nothing. Storage is content-addressed (`images/<sha256>.png`), so two people holding the same image cost two rows and one object.

**Removal archives the record and leaves the bytes alone.** Nothing in this system is permanently deleted, and the object may be shared with another user's row — erasing it would break a record the request never looked at.

**This example is the client's own:** *"a broker (mark) makes a commission with us, we need to give him a 1099 tax form. I want to be able to add that form into his own personal folder."* Passing `ownerUserId` is what files it there.

It stays **PRIVATE** because that is the default. Mark can read it and so can an administrator; another broker of identical rank gets a **404, not a 403** — a 403 would confirm the document exists and turn a list of user ids into a register of who has been paid.

A file whose bytes are plain text is stored as `text/plain` whatever it was named — so HTML uploaded as `invoice.pdf` is stored as text and served as an **attachment** with `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, which means a browser downloads it instead of executing it on this API's origin.

item.name: 12 · Notes
item.description:
Dated entries on a record's timeline — the client's adjustment #5: *"in the trip section and client CRM section, I want to make sure there is a section where I can write notes and add it to a timeline"*.

**`Client.notes` was not that.** It is one string, and editing it destroys what it said before. That field stays as the standing summary the detail sidebar shows — what you need to know about this person — and these are the append-only record of what happened and when. Two questions, two places.

**Polymorphic.** `subjectType` + `subjectId`, so Trips get a timeline by adding one enum value rather than a second table with its own columns, its own permissions and its own screen to keep in step. `subjectId` is therefore not a foreign key the database can check — the service asks the module that owns the subject instead, which is what makes "you may read this note if you may read its client" true rather than merely intended.

**No permissions of its own.** These routes carry no `@RequirePermissions` decorator, the same deliberate choice `11 · Uploads` records: the right to read or write a note is the right to read or write the record it hangs on, and which permission that is depends on a value in the query string, which a decorator cannot see. Authentication is still global.

Every request below is signed in as the seeded SUPER_ADMIN by the folder's pre-request script, except the 403 examples, captured as the seeded broker and assistant.

query.description: **Required.** Allowed (case-sensitive): CLIENT. Lower-case returns 400 rather than being silently corrected.
**Required.** uuid of the record whose notes these are. A record you may not read answers 404, not 403 — a 403 would confirm it exists.
Page number, 1-based. Integer ≥1. Default 1.
Rows per page. Integer 1-100. Default 10. >100 or <1 → 400.
Allowed (case-sensitive): NOTE | EVENT. Absent returns both, which is the point of the endpoint.

request.description:
A record's timeline: what people wrote and what the system recorded, interleaved newest-first (client adjustment #5).

**A timeline of hand-written notes alone would be half a timeline.** Status changes, reassignments and archives are already in the audit trail, and they are the entries nobody has to remember to type — so both are read together. Each row carries `kind`: `NOTE` for something a person wrote, `EVENT` for something the system recorded.

**Withdrawn notes are excluded.** Taking a note off the record is what withdrawing it meant; replaying it beside the events it was withdrawn from would say the opposite. The withdrawn half is `02 · List notes` with `archived=true`.

Paginated across two tables without a UNION: the API takes `skip + take` rows from each source and merges. That is exact rather than approximate — the nth newest row overall cannot be older than the nth newest of either source.

request.description:
Adds a dated entry to a record's timeline.

**Needs write access to the subject, not to notes.** A note carries no permission of its own — the right to write one is the right to edit the record it hangs on. So an assistant, who may read a client and not edit one, reads the timeline and cannot add to it (403), and a broker gets 404 on a client that is not theirs.

`visibility` defaults to **INTERNAL**, the same direction upload visibility defaults to PRIVATE: the cost of failing closed is somebody asking why an agent cannot see an update, and the cost of failing open is desk commentary reaching the person who referred the client.

item.name: 13 · Client Credits
item.description:
Money a client has on account with us — the client's adjustment #9: *"a section on their profile that says credit/money on account ... we can enter how much that is and can always edit that number or select if it was used towards another trip"*.

**This is a ledger, not that number, and the difference is deliberate.** The two halves of his own sentence — "edit that number" and "used towards another trip" — are *credits* and *applications*: movements, with a balance derived from them. A single editable field loses why it changed, and a balance dropping from $18,000 to $6,000 with nothing saying which trip consumed it is an argument waiting to happen. He gets the edit he asked for, on a row, plus an audit trail he did not know to ask for.

**There is no `balance` column.** It is summed on every read, in one place, exactly as a quote's total is — a stored figure beside the parts it is computed from contradicts them the first time one is edited.

**No trip link yet.** Trips do not exist, and a reference string pointing at nothing would become a migration and a set of broken joins the day the table arrives. `reason` carries it for now.

**Reading needs `VIEW_FINANCIALS` *and* access to the client.** An assistant holds the first at NONE and never learns what a client is holding; a broker sees only their own clients, and another broker's ledger answers 404 rather than 403.

Every request below is signed in as the seeded SUPER_ADMIN by the folder's pre-request script, except the 403 examples, captured as the seeded assistant.

item.name: 01 · What the client has on account

query.description: **Required.** uuid of the client whose account this is. A client you may not read answers 404, not 403 — a 403 would confirm they exist, and a balance should not help anyone build a list of client ids.

request.description:
The figures above the ledger: `balance`, `credited`, `applied`, how many movements there are and when the last one was.

**Summed on every read and never stored.** There is no `balance` column, for the same reason a quote has no stored total: the day an edit moves one entry and the stored figure does not follow, the record contradicts itself and nothing on screen says which half is right.

Withdrawn movements count towards nothing here, so the total always agrees with the rows printed underneath it.

Reading any of this needs `VIEW_FINANCIALS`: an assistant never learns what a client is holding, even for a client they can otherwise read.

}

request.description:
The *"can always edit that number"* half of the request — on an entry, which is what gives it an audit trail the client did not know to ask for.

**The balance is re-checked without this row.** Raising an application is measured against what the account actually holds, rather than against a figure that still contains the old value.

`clientId` cannot be changed: money does not move between clients. An entry filed against the wrong one is withdrawn and re-entered, which leaves the mistake visible on both ledgers instead of silently moving a balance.

request.description:
**200, not 201** — a restore creates nothing; it clears a deletion stamp on a row that existed all along.

**The balance is re-checked, because the ledger has moved on.** A $12,000 application withdrawn in March and restored in June lands on whatever the account holds now; if the credit behind it was spent meanwhile, restoring would overdraw the client. A guard that a withdraw-and-restore walks around is not a guard.

request.description:
A run is a demonstration, not a data entry session — and a ledger is the last place to leave debris.

Request 08 restores the movement to show that restore works, which leaves it live, so every run would add money to a real client's account. This withdraws it again, and its test withdraws the credit from request 03 as well. There is no hard delete by design, so archiving the probes is the correct end state.

exec: if (err) { console.warn('teardown could not withdraw ' + credit, err); }
* Signs this folder in as the seeded SUPER_ADMIN.
* Runs before every request in the folder but only acts when the
* current session is for a different account, so it costs one login
* per run rather than one per request. `pm.variables` is run-scoped,
* so a fresh run always re-authenticates.
* This is why no folder below `01 · Auth` contains a login request:
* auth endpoints are documented once, in one place.
if (err) { console.error('session setup failed', err); return; }
// security@ has two-factor on, so a password alone leaves the
// session incomplete. Finish the challenge before continuing,
// or every request in the folder 401s.
body: { mode: 'raw', raw: JSON.stringify({ code: code }) },
// Writes need X-CSRF-Token, and the value is only readable from the
// Parsed out of Set-Cookie rather than read from pm.cookies.jar():
// the jar is not reliably populated in Newman, and a jar read that
// comes back empty would clobber a working token with undefined.
